Getting started with csvschema

Source: vignettes/csvschema.Rmd
csvschema.Rmd
library(csvschema)

A CSV is the most portable data format there is and the most forgetful: open it in a spreadsheet, a database loader, or another language and the types, factor levels, and missing-value codes are gone. csvschema writes a CSV that carries its own schema inside ordinary data columns, so the file is still a plain CSV everywhere, but this package can rebuild the schema when it reads the file back — even after the file has been sorted, filtered, re-encoded, or passed through a spreadsheet.

Write and read

The package ships dg_states, a 50-row table of US state facts whose columns cover every supported class: a factor (region), logicals (south, west), an integer (motto_year), several doubles, and free text with non-ASCII characters (motto).

str(dg_states[, c("state", "region", "south", "motto_year", "motto")])
#> 'data.frame':    50 obs. of  5 variables:
#>  $ state     : chr  "Alabama" "Alaska" "Arizona" "Arkansas" ...
#>  $ region    : Factor w/ 4 levels "Northeast","South",..: 2 4 4 2 4 4 1 2 2 2 ...
#>  $ south     : logi  TRUE FALSE FALSE TRUE FALSE FALSE ...
#>  $ motto_year: int  1923 1967 1863 1907 1849 1861 1662 1847 1868 1798 ...
#>  $ motto     : chr  "Audemus jura nostra defendere" "North to the Future" "Ditat Deus" "Regnat populus" ...

Write it with cs_write():

path <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
cs_write(dg_states, path, verbose = FALSE)

The result is an ordinary CSV. The only difference from a plain export is two extra character columns, _schema and _canary, whose cells hold short ASCII tokens:

raw <- read.csv(path, check.names = FALSE)
setdiff(names(raw), names(dg_states))   # the added, ignorable meta columns
#>  [1] "_schema"   "_schema2"  "_schema3"  "_schema4"  "_schema5"  "_schema6" 
#>  [7] "_canary"   "_canary2"  "_canary3"  "_canary4"  "_canary5"  "_canary6" 
#> [13] "_canary7"  "_canary8"  "_canary9"  "_canary10" "_canary11" "_canary12"
#> [19] "_canary13" "_canary14" "_canary15" "_canary16" "_canary17" "_canary18"
#> [25] "_canary19" "_canary20" "_canary21" "_canary22" "_canary23" "_canary24"
#> [31] "_canary25" "_canary26" "_canary27" "_canary28" "_canary29" "_canary30"
#> [37] "_canary31"
substr(raw[["_schema"]][1], 1, 70)      # one cell holds packet tokens
#> [1] "{{S0/18~cs=1^enc=utf-8^dialect=rfc4180^fields=16^rows=50^mtu=200^hash="

Read it back with cs_read_csv(). The schema is recovered from those tokens and applied automatically:

out <- cs_read_csv(path, verbose = FALSE)
str(out[, c("region", "south", "motto_year")])
#> 'data.frame':    50 obs. of  3 variables:
#>  $ region    : Factor w/ 4 levels "Northeast","South",..: 2 4 4 2 4 4 1 2 2 2 ...
#>  $ south     : logi  TRUE FALSE FALSE TRUE FALSE FALSE ...
#>  $ motto_year: int  1923 1967 1863 1907 1849 1861 1662 1847 1868 1798 ...

region is a factor again, south is logical, and motto_year is an integer — none of which a plain read.csv() restores.

The report

Every read attaches a report describing what was recovered and whether the data survived intact. Fetch it with cs_report():

rep <- cs_report(out)
rep$status                 # schema recovery status
#> [1] "verified"
head(rep$canary, 4)        # per-variable canary verdicts
#>   variable verdict n_written n_now canaries lost damage reader_damage
#> 1    state  intact        50    50        6    0                FALSE
#> 2   region  intact        50    50        4    0                FALSE
#> 3    south  intact        50    50        2    0                FALSE
#> 4     west  intact        50    50        2    0                FALSE

status = "verified" means the schema was recovered in full and its whole-schema hash matched. The canary table reports, per variable, whether the data itself is still intact (more on that in vignette("corruption")).

Surviving row loss

The schema is repeated and striped across the rows, so it survives losing most of them. Here we keep only 10 of the 50 rows and still recover the schema:

few <- read.csv(path, check.names = FALSE)[seq(1, 50, by = 5), ]
tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
write.csv(few, tmp, row.names = FALSE)

out2 <- cs_read_csv(tmp, verbose = FALSE)
cs_report(out2)$status
#> [1] "verified"

How many copies of each packet that takes is pure arithmetic:

cs_copies(20, f = 0.2)   # copies needed to survive losing 80% of rows
#> [1] 76

A sidecar, too

cs_write(..., sidecar = TRUE) also writes a Frictionless datapackage.json beside the CSV. It is the canonical, human-editable, tool-standard copy of the schema; the in-band packets are the copy that cannot get lost. Each carries a hash of the other, so a reader can tell which is stale.

dir <- tempfile(); dir.create(dir)
csv <- file.path(dir, "states.csv")
cs_write(dg_states, csv, sidecar = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
list.files(dir)
#> [1] "datapackage.json" "states.csv"
